26 MB at idle.

Terminal Decline is a terminal for macOS, written in Rust and drawn with Metal. A 100 MB file goes through cat in 0.58 s. Ghostty and kitty are in the charts.

Measured 2 November 2026 on an Apple M1 Max, medians of 5 runs. Full method.

2 November 2026, Apple M1 Max, macOS 27.0. Menlo 13, a 100×30 window with 10k lines of scrollback, one window. Memory is macOS physical footprint summed over all of the terminal's processes. Medians of 5 runs, taken in turns, on a Mac with other work running (load 3 to 6, which is to say an ordinary afternoon).

Ghostty 1.4.0, kitty 0.49.2. The builds measured, the script and the full table are in the README.

Idle, Decline woke 0.5 times a second, as Ghostty did, and kitty 24. Decline's 0.02% CPU is not zero.

An earlier run on 30 October, which also had Warp and Terminal.app in it, is kept apart and not merged into these numbers. In that one Decline idled at 31.5 MB and took 0.61 s for the cat, and Ghostty's cat was quicker, at 0.53 s. Warp (running two windows) took 3.6 s and Terminal.app 4.0 s. None of these runs compared input latency between terminals. The 30 October write-up has that table.

One command, and rush is an app in the Dock.

decline pin rush --dock

A command example, not output. It needs rush, the terminal app for coding agents, installed separately with brew install 0xdeafcafe/tap/rush.

That writes ~/Applications/rush.app and puts it in the Dock. Click it and a Decline window opens running rush, nothing else. A pin keeps its own settings, a config layer of its own (decline pin --edit rush), and --list and --remove do what they say. Pins load the installed app, so they keep working after Decline updates.

The icon is rush's own if it ships one: an app bundle's, or rush.png or rush.icns beside the program. Otherwise Decline draws one, a large initial over the Slope on one of ten fixed hues, picked by a hash of the name. --icon FILE picks something else.

32 px
16 px

Generated pins, artwork rather than a photo of a Dock.

Every match comes with its description.

Decline asks zsh for its completions, then adds a description to each flag and subcommand from the man page or the program's --help. The terminal draws the list itself, in your font and theme.

Grey text after the cursor shows the rest of the first match, and Right takes it. Ctrl+Space opens the list at once. Having it open as you type is a setting (completion_as_you_type), off by default.

The matches come from zsh. This page makes no promise about other shells.

Agents get a real terminal, without a window.

decline ctl starts a program in a Decline terminal that has no window. An agent, or a test, types into it, waits for text or for the command to finish, and reads the screen back: as text, or as JSON with every cell, its colours, the cursor and the modes. A screenshot is drawn on the GPU with your fonts and theme.

It talks to the running app, or starts a headless server with no Dock icon that leaves once it is idle. The socket is reachable only by your user, and agent_api = false turns the whole thing off. A terminal nothing has asked about for 30 minutes is killed. There is no assistant inside decline. It is a terminal for yours to drive.

The details are in the ctl design notes.

terminal-decline ctl spawn --name top --size 100x30 -- htop
terminal-decline ctl wait-for top --text "Load average" --timeout 5000
terminal-decline ctl screen top --json
terminal-decline ctl screenshot top top.png
terminal-decline ctl kill top

terminal-decline ctl spawn --name sh --shell
terminal-decline ctl send sh --text "make test" --key enter
terminal-decline ctl wait-for sh --command --timeout 600000

Command examples, not a captured session. Each prints one line of JSON and exits 0 when done, 3 when a wait timed out.

Install

brew install --cask 0xdeafcafe/tap/terminal-decline

Apple Silicon, macOS 14 Sonoma or later. That installs Terminal Decline.app and the command as both terminal-decline and decline. MIT licence.

From source: clone the repository and run scripts/dogfood.sh --open, which builds a release, makes and signs the app bundle and installs it in ~/Applications. cargo install gives the bare command without the bundle, so no Dock pins from the app. The README has both routes in full.

The in-app updater only offers signed and notarised releases, and there are none yet.
